items.title: Left Ventricular Unloading With Self-Expanding Pump During Venoarterial Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation in Acute Myocardial Infarction.
items.abstract: Increased left ventricular (LV) afterload and distension during venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) support may impede myocardial perfusion in acute myocardial infarction (AMI). Active LV unloading has been associated with improved outcomes. We report the first clinical use of a self-expanding percutaneous ventricular assist device (NyokAssist; magAssist, Suzhou, China) for LV unloading during VA-ECMO in a 56 year old man with AMI-related cardiogenic shock (CS). Successful coronary angiography and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) of the culprit left circumflex (LCx) lesion were performed with NyokAssist + VA-ECMO support. The patient was successfully weaned from VA-ECMO on post-procedure day 5 and remained on NyokAssist support alone for an additional 7 days before being transferred on VA-ECMO to a heart transplant center for consideration of advanced heart failure therapies due to limited myocardial recovery. No device-related complications were observed. This case demonstrates the technical feasibility of early implementation of a combined VA-ECMO and NyokAssist support strategy, enabling LV unloading, temporary hemodynamic stabilization, end-organ improvement, and VA-ECMO decannulation in a patient with AMI-related CS. As this report describes a single-patient experience, further clinical studies are warranted to define the safety, efficacy, and potential role of the use of NyokAssist in combination with VA-ECMO in the management of AMI-related CS.

items.title: Supramolecular Matrine-Proanthocyanidins Nanocomplex-Integrated Carboxymethyl Chitosan Hydrogel with Phenylboronic Acid Modification for Atopic Dermatitis Therapy.
items.abstract: Atopic dermatitis (AD) is a chronic inflammatory skin disease featured by immune dysregulation, oxidative stress, and an impaired epidermal barrier. Oxidative stress and inflammation establish a self-sustaining vicious cycle that accelerates the progression of atopic dermatitis. However, few naturally derived self-assembled nanohydrogels have been developed to disrupt this reciprocal loop for the treatment of cutaneous AD. In this study, matrine (MAT) and proanthocyanidins (PAC), two Chinese medicine-derived molecules with inherent antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activities, co-assembled spontaneously into nanoparticles (PM NPs) in aqueous solution. Incorporation of PM NPs into the phenylboronic acid-modified carboxymethyl chitosan (CP) crosslinked network enhanced the mechanical strength of carboxymethyl chitosan, forming a composite hydrogel (CPPM). Spectral results verified that PM NP self-assembly was mediated by hydrogen bonding and π-π stacking. CPPM efficiently scavenged reactive oxygen species (ROS), suppressed the activation of the Ox-CaMKII and NF-κB signaling pathways, and activated Nrf2 to restore epidermal redox homeostasis. CPPM exhibited favorable moisturizing capacity, appropriate rheological properties, and mild ROS-triggered release to realize local therapeutic effects. In 1-chloro-2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene (DNCB)-induced AD mice, topical CPPM application significantly alleviated epidermal hyperplasia, itching, and inflammatory cytokine expression without obvious toxicity. This self-assembled bioactive hydrogel can concurrently regulate oxidative stress and inflammatory responses, offering a promising topical therapeutic approach against AD.

items.title: Task Force 11: Additional Cardiac Conditions and Considerations in Competitive Athletes.
items.abstract: The recently updated AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes with Cardiovascular Abnormalities provides a comprehensive framework for guiding clinicians in the evaluation and management of competitive athletes. Divided into 11 Task Forces, it covers a broad range of cardiovascular diseases and clinical scenarios. Task Force 11 was devoted to cardiac conditions and considerations in athletes not included in the other Task Forces. Here, we present the detailed rationale for the clinical considerations covered in this section of the Scientific Statement. These topics include hypertension, commotio cordis, pulmonary embolism, performance-enhancing drugs and supplements, exercise in extreme environments (specifically altitude and scuba diving), and pregnancy.
items.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

items.title: Task Force 10: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Masters Athletes with Underlying Cardiovascular Disease.
items.abstract: Masters athletes are individuals ≥35 yr of age who place a high premium on exercise training and competition. This document details important cardiovascular conditions, risk factors, and data-driven discussion, which serve as the rationale for Section X from the 2025 AHA/ACC Scientific Statement: Clinical Considerations for Competitive Sports Participation for Athletes Cardiovascular Abnormalities. Disease-specific risk stratification and shared decision-making are the cornerstones for Masters athletes when considering competitive sports participation. Coronary artery disease, atrial fibrillation, incidental myocardial fibrosis, aortic enlargement and aneurysms, and valvular heart disease are included in this Task Force document.
items.journal: Medicine and science in sports and exercise

items.title: Task Force 9: Clinical Considerations for the Care of Athletes with Cardiac Channelopathies.
items.abstract: Cardiac channelopathies, including long QT syndrome, catecholaminergic polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, Brugada syndrome, and short QT syndrome, are heterogeneous conditions, which can lead to varying risks in athletes depending on their symptoms, disease severity, genotype, and therapies initiated. Historically, athletes with these conditions were excluded from participation with blanket restrictions, despite an absence of data. More recently, a number of studies have provided more scientific evidence to guide decision making and have been incorporated into these guidelines for athletes with cardiac channelopathies. Many athletes with these conditions may be supported in their decision to return to play as part of a shared decision-making model when they have been assessed, risk stratified, and appropriately treated by a specialist with expertise in these conditions.

items.title: Molecular Profiling for Precision Medicine in Adrenocortical Carcinoma: Real-World Data From the French Network ENDOCAN-COMETE.
items.abstract: Adrenocortical carcinoma (ACC) is a rare tumor with poor prognosis. Precision medicine and molecularly matched treatment (MMT) represent a new opportunity in oncology. We conducted a retrospective study of patients with advanced ACC within the French ENDOCAN COMETE network from 2009 to 2022 who have been providing access to molecular profiling (MP). We investigated the benefits of the MMT strategy in terms of response according to RECIST, median progression-free survival (PFS), overall survival (OS), and growth modulation index (GMI). We enrolled 78 patients with ACC who underwent MP of the primary tumor in 41 patients. Most patients had metastasis at diagnosis, with at least one GRAS criterion. P53 alteration and activation of the Wnt/β-catenin pathway were the most frequent genetic alterations. No mutations were found in 20.5% of patients' tumors. The microsatellite instability phenotype was present in two cases. The median OS from the date of first metastasis was 33.3 months (95% CI, 24.7 to 56.2) with most patients receiving platinum-based chemotherapy and mitotane as first-line therapy. Twelve patients were treated with MMT as a second- or third-line therapy. An objective response rate was observed in two patients with a complete response under immunotherapy. The median PFS with MMT was 2.5 months. The mean GMI was 1.02, above 1.3 in three patients (4%). Molecular alteration-based precision medicine is associated with potential antitumor benefits in a limited subset of patients with ACC.

items.title: Identifying Predictive Biomarkers of Resistance in Patients With Breast Cancer.
items.abstract: Residual cancer burden (RCB) after neoadjuvant chemotherapy is highly prognostic of disease-free survival in patients with high-risk early-stage breast cancer, and extensive residual disease (RCBIII) indicates treatment resistance. Identifying intrinsic pretreatment resistance may enable earlier redirection to therapies more likely to achieve pathologic complete response. We aimed to identify molecular biomarkers associated with resistance to neoadjuvant therapies, develop predictive models, and create an interactive resource. We analyzed pretreatment transcriptomic data from 987 patients with stage II to III breast cancer enrolled in the randomized, adaptive, multiarm phase II I-SPY2 trial. We applied the response-weighted elastic net algorithm (RWEN) to identify gene expression signatures associated with poor response (RCBIII) versus good response (RCB0/I). Using these gene sets, we trained random forest (RF) models to predict response and benchmarked them against models trained using randomly sampled gene sets. To evaluate robustness, RWEN-derived gene sets were evaluated in 1,127 nonoverlapping validation I-SPY2 cohorts, including independent paclitaxel control arms, paclitaxel plus immunotherapy arms, and receptor subtype-matched patient subsets. We derived resistance-associated gene sets across nine treatment arms and receptor subtypes, implicating immune evasion, chromatin remodeling, DNA repair deficiency, and human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) signaling. In the validation cohort, models using the paclitaxel gene set achieved sensitivity = 0.88/specificity = 0.65; models using the pembrolizumab gene set across immunotherapy-containing arms achieved sensitivity = 0.78/specificity = 0.69; models using subtype-specific gene sets achieved sensitivity = 0.61-0.71/specificity = 0.65-0.74 across hormone receptor-positive, and triple-negative gene sets. We make public ISPY_Explore which enables visualization of gene and protein expression by treatment arm, receptor subtype, and response. This integrative approach identified biologically diverse resistance-associated gene sets with predictive and translational potential. ISPY_Explore provides a cloud-based tool for exploring molecular data and may guide the development of personalized treatment strategies to overcome resistance in high-risk breast cancer.

items.title: Early Treatment Failure in Patients With Relapsed/Refractory Multiple Myeloma Receiving Bispecific T-Cell Engagers: Development and Validation of the CHARGE Prognostic Index.
items.abstract: Outcomes with bispecific T-cell engagers (TCEs) in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma (RRMM) are heterogeneous. A practical tool to guide prognosis is needed. We developed a model integrating clinical, biological, and treatment-related variables to predict progression-free survival (PFS) in patients receiving B-cell maturation antigen (BCMA)- or G-protein-coupled receptor class 5 member D-directed TCEs. We evaluated outcomes of 577 BCMA-directed and 366 talquetamab treatments across 15 US Multiple Myeloma Immunotherapy Consortium centers. Variables significantly associated with inferior PFS in a multivariate Cox model were incorporated into a prognostic score and validated in an independent multicenter International Myeloma Foundation cohort. With a median follow-up of 8.4 months, the median PFS was 6.4 months (7.0 months for BCMA TCE; 6.1 months for talquetamab); 92% of patients were triple-class-refractory. Six variables significantly associated with inferior PFS-high-risk cytogenetic abnormalities (HRCAs) [del(17p) or ≥2 HRCAs], hyperferritinemia (≥600 ng/mL), anemia (hemoglobin CHARGE index, stratifying patients into three risk groups. The median PFS was 21.8 months (95% CI, 11.7 to not reached), 7.1 months (95% CI, 6.1 to 10.1), and 1.6 months (95% CI, 1.2 to 2.5) in the low-, intermediate-, and high-risk groups, respectively; hazard ratios (HRs) were 2.0 (95% CI, 1.5 to 2.7) and 4.8 (95% CI, 3.5 to 6.7) for intermediate- and high-risk versus low-risk groups. External validation (n = 173) showed that the median PFS was not reached, 7.0 months, and 3.0 months, with corresponding HRs of 2.9 (95% CI, 1.7 to 4.9) and 4.8 (95% CI, 2.6 to 8.7). The CHARGE index provides a simplified and externally validated framework for predicting treatment outcomes in patients with RRMM receiving TCEs.
items.journal: Journal of clinical oncology : official journal of the American Society of Clinical Oncology

items.title: No "Co" for CD28 in NK cells: CD28-harnessed natural killer cells mediate APC lysis independently of T-cell receptor presence or engagement.
items.abstract: Recently, primary natural killer (NK) cells have been engineered to express a transgenic T-cell receptor (NK:TCR), enabling recognition of intracellular and extracellular tumor antigens via HLA-restricted presentation. While this strategy broadens antigen specificity, NK cells lack canonical co-stimulatory receptors required for optimal T-cell activation. In T cells, CD28 engagement with CD80 and CD86 provides the essential "signal 2" that drives proliferation, differentiation, and cytokine production. We therefore examined whether expression of wild-type CD28 could facilitate co-stimulatory function to NK:TCR cells. Wild-type CD28 was introduced into NK-92 NFAT reporter cells and primary NK cells to assess its activity in the absence of TCR signaling. In parallel, CD28 was co-expressed with either relevant or irrelevant TCRs to evaluate its role in TCR-mediated responses. Our results show that CD28 signaling in NK cells differs from its role in T cells. CD28 functioned as a primary activating receptor, inducing activation upon interaction with CD80 or CD86 even in the absence of TCR engagement, resulting in the lysis of CD80- and/or CD86-positive cells, including antigen-presenting cells. This effect required the intracellular signaling domain of CD28. Blocking experiments demonstrated that both CD80 and CD86 are sufficient to drive activation, with no evidence for additional ligands. Notably, the presence of an irrelevant TCR did not restrain CD28-driven activation. These findings reveal fundamental differences in CD28-mediated signaling between NK and T cells and highlight a potential safety concern for NK-based therapies, as full-length CD28 expression may promote TCR-independent activation and cytotoxicity toward CD80/CD86-expressing cells.

items.title: Engineering exhaustion-resistance CD19 CAR T cells to address translational barriers for the treatment of cancer and autoimmune disease.
items.abstract: PRGN-3008 is a CD19 CAR T cell designed to overcome key limitations in ex vivo and in vivo CAR T manufacturing, cost, safety, and therapeutic durability. Featuring decentralized overnight manufacturing without ex vivo expansion, PRGN-3008 is engineered using a single nonviral transposon to encode CD19 CAR, membrane-bound interleukin-15 (mbIL-15) for improved persistence, PD-1-targeting microRNAs to prevent exhaustion, and an inducible safety switch for controlled in vivo elimination. Safety studies showed low vector copy numbers, favorable integration profile, and efficient CAR T ablation upon safety-switch activation. The combined mbIL-15 expression and PD-1 down-regulation preserved PRGN-3008 polyfunctionality and sustained cytotoxicity across repeated tumor challenges, outperforming nonarmored or singly modified CAR T cells. In xenograft models, overnight-manufactured PRGN-3008 without ex vivo expansion and activation achieved durable tumor clearance, prolonged tumor-free survival, robust antigen dependent expansion, and enrichment of memory T cell phenotypes linked to clinical durability. Notably, PRGN-3008 generated from heavily pretreated patients with systemic lupus erythematosus or lupus nephritis, maintained effector function, resisted terminal differentiation under chronic antigen exposure, and effectively depleted autoreactive B cells in a humanized mouse model. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that the combination of mbIL-15 expression and PD-1 down-regulation enhances the expression of genes associated with bioenergetic pathways, including oxidative phosphorylation, mitochondrial biogenesis, glycolysis, and glutamine utilization, thereby supporting resistance to exhaustion and sustained effector function. Collectively, these data support PRGN-3008 as a clinically translatable, scalable, and controllable CAR T with the potential to expand access to cell therapy across oncology and autoimmune indications.

items.title: CHD4 promotes hepatitis B virus transcription by facilitating RNA polymerase II recruitment to cccDNA.
items.abstract: Chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection remains a major global health burden, largely due to the persistence of covalently closed circular DNA (cccDNA), which serves as the template for viral transcription. Although host factors involved in regulating cccDNA transcription have been increasingly recognized, the molecular mechanisms controlling HBV minichromosome activity remain incompletely understood. Chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 4 (CHD4), the catalytic component of the nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase (NuRD) complex, is a key regulator of chromatin remodeling and transcriptional regulation. In this study, we demonstrate that CHD4 facilitates efficient HBV transcription. Depletion of CHD4 in HBV-infected hepatoma cells markedly reduced viral RNA levels and antigen production without affecting HBV uptake, nuclear import, cccDNA establishment, or cccDNA stability. Mechanistically, CHD4 was recruited to HBV cccDNA and promoted the occupancy of RNA polymerase II (RNA Pol II) on the viral minichromosome. Loss of CHD4 impaired RNA Pol II recruitment to cccDNA, resulting in reduced viral transcription. Furthermore, domain mapping identified the CT2 region of CHD4 as essential for its interaction with RNA Pol II. Collectively, our findings reveal a previously unrecognized role of CHD4 in regulating HBV cccDNA transcription and establish CHD4-mediated RNA Pol II recruitment as a critical mechanism controlling HBV gene expression.IMPORTANCEHepatitis B virus (HBV) infection affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide and can lead to severe liver diseases, including cirrhosis and liver cancer. A major challenge in curing HBV infection is the persistence of a stable viral DNA structure inside infected liver cells that continuously produces viral components. Understanding how this viral DNA is controlled by host cells is essential for developing new therapeutic strategies. In this study, we identified chromodomain helicase DNA-binding protein 4 (CHD4) as a host factor that supports HBV gene production by helping the virus recruit the cellular machinery required for viral RNA synthesis. Our findings reveal a previously unrecognized mechanism by which human liver cells regulate HBV persistence and provide new insights into virus-host interactions that may guide future approaches to achieve durable HBV control.

items.title: Dysregulated apoptosis in the spleen from patients with splenomegaly due to cirrhosis.
items.abstract: Splenomegaly (SM) secondary to portal hypertension is characterized by the pathological enlargement of the spleen due to chronically elevated portal venous pressure. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying its pathogenesis remain largely unclear. AND M: ETHODS: Sixteen patients with hepatitis B-related liver cirrhosis and SM who underwent subtotal splenectomy with omental plasty and retroperitoneal fixation were enrolled in the SM group, whereas 15 patients who underwent splenectomy for traumatic splenic rupture (without SM) served as the traumatic splenic rupture control (TSRC) group. Splenic tissue samples were collected for hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) assay, immunohistochemistry (IHC), quantitative reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction, and Western blotting (WB). H&E staining revealed dilated red pulp, fibrotic splenic cords, atrophic white pulp, and a thickened splenic capsule in the SM group. A significant increase in the proportion of apoptotic cells was noted in the spleens of patients with SM. Moreover, differences were observed in apoptotic protein expression assessed by IHC between the two groups. The expression of apoptosis-related genes, including BAX, CASP3, and CASP9, was significantly upregulated, whereas BCL2 expression was significantly reduced in the SM group. WB confirmed that the levels of BAX, cleaved CASP3, and cleaved CASP9 were elevated in the SM group, whereas splenic BCL2 expression was below the detection limit in both groups. Apoptosis was dysregulated in the spleen of patients with portal hypertension-associated SM secondary to liver cirrhosis. Our findings suggest that SM contributes to a pro-apoptotic environment in the spleen of patients with liver cirrhosis.

items.title: Berry contagious: Use of post-exposure prophylaxis to respond to an outbreak of hepatitis A associated with frozen imported berries in Canada.
items.abstract: In April 2016, the Public Health Agency of Canada received reports of three locally-acquired cases of hepatitis A in one province who reported consuming frozen berries sold by a common retail chain. Subsequently, cases of hepatitis A with frozen berry consumption in other provinces were reported, and all illness onsets were within an eight-week period. To conduct a national outbreak investigation with provincial and federal partners to identify the source, and determine appropriate public health measures. Epidemiological data were collected through case interviews and purchase history records were obtained from the retailer. Hepatitis A virus (HAV) genotyping and ribonucleic acid (RNA) fingerprinting identified outbreak-related cases. The food safety investigation included traceback, traceforward, and testing of the suspected product. Of the 25 confirmed cases, 21 were genotyped, revealing a multi-strain outbreak: 16 were genotype 1B with identical RNA fingerprints; and five cases were genotype 1A with nearly identical RNA fingerprints. Epidemiologic evidence implicated a frozen berry blend (Product A). Hepatitis A virus was detected in a closed retail sample, an open sample from a case's home and a blackberry input. Product A was recalled, and post-exposure prophylaxis was offered. More than 11,000 people were vaccinated by the retailer and public health units. In September 2016, a new cluster of hepatitis A cases matching the outbreak strain was identified; the index case had consumed recalled product. Rapid epidemiologic investigation, purchase history records, traceback evidence, retailer cooperation and collaboration between public health partners facilitated rapid identification and product recall.

items.title: Carrier-free Arg-CpG augments antitumor efficacy by triggering specific immune activation.
items.abstract: The delivery of nucleic acids using nonviral vectors represents a promising approach for cancer therapy. Nevertheless, nucleic acid-based drugs suffer from poor potency and rapid degradation. Herein, we report a carrier-free nucleic acid delivery system termed Arg-CpG, which is easily constructed through charge-driven assembly of poly(l-arginine) (Arg) and the immune adjuvant unmethylated cytosine-phosphate-guanine oligonucleotide (CpG). This Arg-CpG functions as both a carrier and a therapeutic agent, thereby eliminating the need for a conventional drug delivery vehicle and minimizing potential toxicity. The guanidinium groups of Arg endow Arg-CpG with dual functionalities: enhancing cellular uptake and serving as the nitrogen donor for iNOS-mediated nitric oxide (NO) generation. This NO production further synergizes with CpG to drive macrophage reprogramming toward an antitumor phenotype. Notably, Arg-CpG exhibits cell-type-dependent modulation of autophagy. It disrupts autophagic machinery in 4T1 tumor cells while preserving functional autophagy in RAW264.7 macrophages. This differential activity results in selective killing of tumor cells without compromising the viability or function of normal immune cells. Consequently, Arg-CpG elicits a robust antitumor immune response in vivo. Moreover, the modular design of Arg-CpG enables its straightforward assembly with CpG oligonucleotides and other nucleic acid payloads (e.g., anti-miR oligonucleotides and siRNA), establishing a versatile and promising platform for nucleic acid-based cancer therapy.

items.title: A novel label-free fluorescence sensing platform for detecting alkaline phosphatase in liver cancer by using SYBR Green I.
items.abstract: Liver cancer is a commonly diagnosed malignancy with a high fatality rate, posing a great threat and burden to human health and life. Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is an essential hydrolase that catalyzes the hydrolysis of the phosphate groups of various substances. It has been reported that the expression level of ALP correlates with hepatocellular carcinoma, making ALP a valuable biomarker for liver cancer diagnosis. Herein, a novel and simple sensing platform is developed for the sensitive, facile, and specific detection of ALP. In this research, a 5'-terminal phosphorylation-modified hairpin DNA structure, termed HP DNA, is employed as the recognition substrate for ALP. In the presence of ALP, it catalyzes the dephosphorylation of HP DNA, thereby protecting HP DNA from λ exonuclease ( λ exo)-mediated digestion. The remaining intact HP DNA subsequently binds SYBR Green I in the reaction system, leading to a markedly enhanced fluorescence signal that enables the quantification of ALP. The proposed method allows for the detection of ALP within 23 min, achieving a LOD of 0.03 U L -1 . Moreover, this label-free fluorescence sensing platform demonstrated sensitive ALP detection in spiked human serum samples, indicating its great potential for biochemical study and clinical detection applications. Although the proposed method exhibits these advantages, challenges remain for ALP detection, including the need for multiplexed analysis of multiple cancer biomarkers and the application in complex clinical specimens. Future efforts should focus on improving the anti-interference capability, simplifying operational procedures, and developing more robust signal transduction strategies to further facilitate clinical translation.

items.title: Global, regional, and national burden of liver cancer attributable to high BMI and hyperglycemia from 1990 to 2021: A systematic analysis of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2021.
items.abstract: To quantify the global, regional, and national burden of liver cancer attributable to high body mass index (BMI) and hyperglycemia from 1990 to 2021 using Global Burden of Disease (GBD) 2021 data, we analyzed GBD 2021 estimates for 204 countries and territories, 21 GBD regions, and 5 Sociodemographic Index (SDI) quintiles. Attributable deaths and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) were estimated using population attributable fractions. Temporal trends were assessed using estimated annual percentage changes (EAPCs), together with age-period-cohort, SDI, frontier, decomposition, and inequality analyses. From 1990 to 2021, global deaths attributable to high BMI increased from 10,282 (95% uncertainty interval [UI], 4196-16,722) to 46,204 (95% UI, 18,606-77,983), while the age-standardized mortality rate (ASMR) increased from 0.26 to 0.53 per 1,00,000 population. The EAPCs for high BMI were 2.37 (95% confidence interval [CI], 2.29-2.45) for ASMR and 2.31 (95% CI, 2.22-2.40) for the age-standardized DALY rate (ASDR). For hyperglycemia, the corresponding EAPCs were 1.90 (95% CI, 1.74-2.05) and 1.65 (95% CI, 1.51-1.79). The fastest increases occurred in South Asia for high BMI and Southern Latin America for hyperglycemia. The burden was generally higher among males and older adults, with substantial geographic and socioeconomic heterogeneity. The liver cancer burden attributable to high BMI and hyperglycemia increased substantially from 1990 to 2021. Integrated metabolic risk reduction and liver cancer prevention strategies are needed, particularly in populations experiencing rapid increases in metabolic risk.

items.title: Visualization of metabolic reprogramming of liver tumors in situ based on mass spectrometry imaging.
items.abstract: Metabolic reprogramming, a hallmark of cancer, has the potential to create therapeutic vulnerabilities. Understanding and exploiting the metabolic differences between developing cancer cells and normal cells plays a crucial role in advancing cancer treatment. In the present study, utilizing temporal stable isotope labeling combined with mass spectrometry imaging (MSI) technology, spatial metabolic maps in the orthotopic liver cancer mouse model were obtained. This approach allowed us to simultaneously visualize the metabolic behavior of both cancerous and paracancerous tissues. Our results revealed a lower content of 13 C-labeled glucose in cancerous tissues compared with paracancerous tissues, together with the distinct isotope-associated signals of endogenous metabolites, including lactate, malate, glutamate, gluconate, and 11,12-epoxyeicosatrienoic acid (11,12-EET). Notably, the isotope-associated signals of lactate, malate, and glutamate were higher in cancerous tissue than in paracancerous tissue, whereas gluconate and 11,12-EET exhibited the opposite trend. These findings suggest a relatively active glycolysis pathway and TCA cycle, and relatively lower PPP-related glucose oxidation in cancerous tissues. Immunofluorescence analysis further characterized the expression patterns of related metabolic enzymes. This approach provides a powerful tool for visualizing the spatial and temporal regulation of metabolic dynamics in cancerous tissues, providing a unique opportunity to study the in situ metabolic reprogramming behavior of cancer.

items.title: Postoperative Management After Curative-Intent Resection of Colorectal Liver Metastases: A Critical Review of Recent Randomized Evidence.
items.abstract: Postoperative management after curative-intent treatment of colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) remains controversial because improvements in recurrence-related outcomes have not consistently translated into longer overall survival (OS). This critical narrative review examines randomized evidence for systemic chemotherapy and hepatic arterial infusion (HAI), together with emerging evidence on circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA). Trial-based findings, prognostic associations, and unvalidated treatment-effect hypotheses were critically distinguished. Postoperative fluoropyrimidine- or oxaliplatin-based treatment can delay recurrence in some settings, but a durable OS benefit has not been consistently demonstrated. Contemporary HAI trials differ in patient selection, regional drugs, systemic therapy, and endpoints. PACHA-01 reported improved hepatic recurrence-free survival in a selected population, HARVEST was terminated early, and PUMP did not meet its primary endpoint. These findings neither establish routine HAI nor identify validated predictors of benefit. Postoperative ctDNA is strongly prognostic, but nonrandomized associations between adjuvant treatment and outcomes cannot establish the clinical utility of ctDNA-directed treatment allocation. A conceptual distinction between hepatic and systemic recurrence risk may support multidisciplinary deliberation and prospective trial design, but should not be used as a validated postoperative treatment-selection algorithm. Clinical decisions must also account for prior chemotherapy, postoperative recovery, toxicity, local treatment opportunities, institutional expertise, and patient preferences.
